Certain regulated carriers question whether any of these benefits will ever accrue to small shippers, for they contend that exempt carriers will limit their operations to lucrative high volume shippers. In the Interim Report we were not persuaded by this argument. In that report we stated that by updating the presently narrow commercial zone limits, local cartage operators should be able to allocate more efficiently their metropolitan area operations so as to serve all revenue producing shippers. We continue to adhere to this view. The problems of small shippers in urban areas are of a different nature than those of small shippers in remote or rural locations. Since the marginal cost of providing service to urban area shippers is less than in sparsely populated rural areas, the access to more carriers caused by expansion of commercial zones and carriers' service areas should enable both large and small shippers to benefit. These views are underscored by the many representations favoring zone expansion filed by suburban shippers of modest size. These shippers feel that they lack the traffic volume, legal expertise, and resources to support an application for motor carrier authority. Finally, the augmentation of freight 66 forwarder terminal areas should improve small shipments service
66 
In the Interim Report we stated:
...
the expansion of freight forwarder terminal areas should ameliorate the service woes of small shippers. Forwarders specialize in the movement of less-than-truckload and less-than-carload traffic, and increasing their terminal areas can only improve small shipments service. Forwarder operations also reduce the disparity in leverage exercised by large and small shippers. While large shippers can demand quality service by virtue of their attractive tonnage, small shippers are handicapped in this respect. The forwarder in its capacity as "agent" for the collective interests of these shippers can obtain superior linehaul service. Commercial Zones, 124 M.C.C. at 181.
